WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Senate Republicans on Tuesday blocked a Democratic initiative to tax the windfall profits oil companies have reaped amid soaring energy prices, with the minority leader dismissing the proposal as a "gimmick." Record energy prices have translated into record profits for oil companies. The measure fell short of the 60 votes required under Senate rules to proceed, with the final tally standing at 51-43. Six Republicans, including three seeking re-election in November, broke with their party to support the bill. Meanwhile, two Democrats—Sen. Mary Landrieu of oil-producing Louisiana and Majority Leader Harry Reid, who cast a procedural "no" vote to preserve his right to bring the measure back to the floor—voted against it.

In addition to imposing a 25 percent windfall tax on oil companies, the bill would have permitted lawsuits against the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and suspended deposits into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Profits derived from renewable energy sources would have been exempt from the tax.

"We're not afraid, on this side, to go after Big Oil when they are not doing the right thing," said Sen. Charles Schumer, D-New York. "And we are not afraid to go after OPEC because they are a cartel that squeezes us. We're not afraid to take strong, tough action—some of which will yield results in the short run, some in the longer run—to bring down the all-too-high price of gasoline."

Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-North Dakota, argued that the measure was necessary to "wring out" speculators he blamed for driving crude oil prices above $130 a barrel in recent weeks.

Senate Republicans, however, countered that the proposed taxes would ultimately harm consumers and diminish America's oil supply, accusing Democrats of engaging in election-year politics. "This bill is, pure and simple, a pathetic attempt to even call itself an energy plan," said Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison, R-Texas.

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell was similarly critical. "Hitting the gas companies might make for good campaign literature or evening news clips, but it won't address the problem," he said. "This bill isn't a serious response to gas prices—it is just a gimmick." The Kentucky Republican added, "They are hoping the idea of going after energy companies will create the illusion of action, after a week in which they themselves fought for a bill that would make the problem worse. What a political charade."

With average gas prices edging above $4 a gallon, the issue looms large in voters' minds. A CNN/Opinion Research Corp. poll released Tuesday found that 40 percent of respondents were more concerned about the cost of gasoline than about long lines at the pump, reminiscent of the energy crisis of the 1970s. Still, 55 percent of those surveyed expressed greater concern about potential long lines and rationing.

The poll reflects telephone interviews conducted with 1,035 adults on Wednesday and Thursday, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points.

CNN's Ted Barrett, Lisa Desjardins, Matt Smith, Virginia Nicolaidis, and Scott J. Anderson contributed to this report.

# Republican Senators Reject Democratic Oil Tax Proposal

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- A Democratic-backed plan to impose taxes on the surplus earnings oil companies have accumulated amid soaring fuel costs was defeated by GOP senators on Tuesday, with the minority party's leader dismissing it as a mere "gimmick." Oil firms have seen unprecedented profits alongside all-time high energy costs. The proposal fell short of the 60-vote threshold necessary under Senate procedure to advance, ultimately losing by a 51-43 margin.

Notably, half a dozen Republicans crossed party lines to back the legislation, including three facing re-election battles this fall. Meanwhile, two Democrats voted against it: Louisiana's Mary Landrieu, whose state has significant oil production interests, and Majority Leader Harry Reid, who strategically voted no in order to preserve his ability to reintroduce the bill later under chamber rules.

Beyond imposing a 25 percent surtax on oil corporations, the legislation would have opened the door for legal action against OPEC, the oil-exporting nations' cartel, and halted contributions to the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Notably, earnings generated from renewable energy would have been exempt from this taxation.

Sen. Charles Schumer (D-New York) defended the approach: "We're not afraid, on this side, to go after Big Oil when they are not doing the right thing. And we are not afraid to go after OPEC because they are a cartel that squeezes us. We're not afraid to do some strong tough things that will—some in the short run, some in the longer run—that will bring down the price, the all too high price, of gasoline."

North Dakota Democrat Byron Dorgan argued the legislation was necessary to eliminate market speculators, whom he held responsible for pushing crude prices past $130 per barrel in recent weeks.

Republicans, however, countered that the tax hikes would ultimately damage consumers and diminish domestic oil production, characterizing the effort as nothing more than election-season theater. Texas Republican Kay Bailey Hutchison called it "pure and simple a pathetic attempt to even call itself an energy plan."

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky was similarly critical: "Hitting the gas companies might make for good campaign literature or evening news clips, but it won't address the problem. This bill isn't a serious response to gas prices. It is just a gimmick." He continued, "They are hoping the idea of going after energy companies will create the illusion of action after a week in which they themselves fought for a bill that would make the problem worse. What a political charade."

With average gas prices climbing past the $4-per-gallon mark, the issue has clearly captured voters' attention. According to a CNN/Opinion Research Corp. survey released Tuesday, 40 percent of respondents said they're more troubled by fuel costs than by the extended lines at gas stations reminiscent of the 1970s energy crisis—though a majority, 55 percent, expressed greater concern about potential rationing and long waits.

The survey, based on phone interviews with 1,035 adults conducted Wednesday and Thursday, carries a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points.

*CNN's Ted Barrett, Lisa Desjardins, Matt Smith, Virginia Nicolaidis and Scott J. Anderson contributed to this report.*

# Senate Republicans Block Windfall Profits Tax on Oil Companies

Senate Republicans successfully blocked a Democratic-sponsored bill on Tuesday that sought to impose a 25 percent windfall profits tax on major oil companies. The measure fell short of the 60 votes required to overcome procedural hurdles and proceed to a full floor debate, with the final tally standing at 51-43 in favor—nine votes shy of the threshold needed for passage.

## Cross-Party Voting Patterns

The vote did not break down entirely along strict party lines. Six Republican senators broke from their party to support the Democratic measure, signaling some bipartisan concern over rising energy costs and corporate profits amid soaring oil prices. Conversely, two Democrats voted against the bill: Senator Mary Landrieu of Louisiana, a state with significant oil industry interests, and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid of Nevada. Reid's opposing vote, however, was largely a procedural maneuver rather than a substantive rejection of the bill's content—by voting with the majority against the measure, he preserved his right under Senate rules to bring the legislation back to the floor for reconsideration at a later date.

## Provisions Beyond the Windfall Tax

The proposed legislation extended well beyond the headline windfall profits tax. Among its other key provisions, the bill would have granted the federal government authority to pursue legal action against OPEC, the international cartel of oil-producing nations, potentially opening the door to antitrust-style litigation against the organization's production and pricing decisions. Additionally, the bill called for a temporary suspension of deposits into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, a move intended to increase the immediate supply of oil available on the open market and potentially ease upward pressure on prices. Notably, the bill included a carve-out for renewable energy companies, explicitly exempting their profits from the proposed tax—a provision designed to encourage continued investment in alternative energy sources even as traditional oil producers faced increased taxation.

## Democratic Justification for the Measure

Senators Charles Schumer of New York and Byron Dorgan of North Dakota emerged as vocal defenders of the legislation, framing it as an essential response to what they characterized as exploitative practices by major oil companies, OPEC, and market speculators. The senators argued that these entities bore significant responsibility for driving crude oil prices above $130 per barrel, a level that was placing substantial strain on American consumers and businesses alike. In their view, the windfall tax represented a necessary corrective measure to address what they saw as unjustified profiteering during a period of economic hardship for ordinary Americans grappling with high gasoline and energy costs.

## Republican Opposition and Criticism

Republican lawmakers, however, offered a starkly different assessment of the bill's merits and motivations. Senators Kay Bailey Hutchison of Texas and Minority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky were among the most prominent critics, dismissing the legislation as little more than an election-year political stunt designed to score points with frustrated voters rather than address the underlying causes of high energy prices. They contended that imposing additional taxes on oil companies would prove counterproductive, ultimately passing increased costs on to consumers already struggling with expensive gasoline. Furthermore, Republican critics warned that such punitive taxation could discourage domestic oil production and exploration, potentially reducing the overall American oil supply at a time when increased production—not additional regulatory burdens—was needed to help stabilize prices and reduce dependence on foreign oil sources.

The failed vote underscored the deep partisan divide over how best to address the energy crisis, with Democrats favoring direct intervention against perceived corporate excess and Republicans advocating for market-based solutions focused on expanding supply.

# Senate Republicans Block Windfall Profits Tax on Oil Companies

Senate Republicans on Thursday blocked a Democratic-led measure that would have imposed a 25 percent windfall profits tax on major oil companies, opened the door for federal lawsuits against OPEC for price manipulation, and temporarily suspended government deposits into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The bill represented the latest attempt by Democrats to respond to soaring gasoline prices and record profits reported by energy companies, an issue that has taken on heightened political significance as the November elections approach.

The legislation failed to clear a key procedural hurdle, falling on a vote of 51 to 43—well short of the 60 votes required to overcome a Republican-led filibuster and proceed to a final vote. The vote broke down largely along party lines, though not entirely: six Republicans broke from their party to support advancing the bill, while two Democrats voted against it, siding with the GOP majority in blocking the measure.

Proponents of the bill argued that with oil companies posting some of the largest quarterly profits in corporate history even as American families struggled with high prices at the pump, it was time for the industry to contribute more back to consumers and to the government. Supporters framed the windfall tax as a matter of fairness, contending that oil companies were reaping extraordinary rewards from market conditions rather than from increased investment or innovation, and that a portion of those profits should be redirected to ease the burden on ordinary Americans.

The provision allowing lawsuits against OPEC was similarly pitched as a tool to hold the oil-producing cartel accountable for practices that Democrats say have artificially inflated prices through production controls. Meanwhile, the suspension of deposits into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve was presented as a short-term mechanism to increase the immediate supply of oil available to the market, thereby helping to ease upward pressure on prices.

Republicans, however, were quick to dismiss the bill as little more than an election-year political maneuver. They argued that the proposal amounted to a "gimmick" designed to score points with voters frustrated by high energy costs rather than a serious attempt to address the underlying causes of price increases. Critics from the GOP contended that imposing a windfall tax would discourage oil companies from investing in new production and exploration, ultimately leading to reduced domestic oil supply. They warned that such a reduction in supply would only exacerbate the very problem the bill purported to solve, driving prices even higher in the long run and placing additional strain on American consumers.

The failure of the bill underscores the deep partisan divide over how to address the country's energy challenges, with Democrats continuing to push for measures targeting industry profits and market practices, while Republicans favor approaches centered on increasing domestic production and reducing regulatory burdens on energy companies. With the vote falling short of the threshold needed to advance, the windfall profits tax and related measures are unlikely to move forward in their current form, though the issue is expected to remain a flashpoint in the broader debate over energy policy as the election season continues.

# Senate Blocks Windfall Profits Tax on Oil Companies

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — The Senate on Tuesday rejected a Democratic proposal to impose a windfall profits tax on major oil companies, dealing a blow to lawmakers who had hoped to use the measure to address soaring gasoline prices that have squeezed American consumers.

The bill, which failed to garner the 60 votes needed to overcome a Republican-led filibuster, would have imposed a 25 percent tax on "unreasonable" profits from the five largest oil companies unless they invested that money in renewable energy sources or expanded refining capacity.

The final vote was 51-43, largely along party lines, with most Republicans opposing the measure and most Democrats supporting it.

"This is nothing short of a moral outrage," said Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nevada, following the vote. "While American families are struggling to fill their gas tanks and heat their homes, big oil companies are posting the largest profits in the history of American business. We simply asked them to pay their fair share."

The bill's supporters pointed to record profits reported by companies including ExxonMobil, which posted a quarterly profit of nearly $11 billion earlier this year — the largest quarterly profit ever reported by a U.S. corporation.

"Exxon made $40 billion in profits last year alone," said Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-New York, one of the bill's chief sponsors. "That's $4.5 million an hour. Meanwhile, American families are being asked to choose between filling their gas tank and buying groceries. This is simply not sustainable, and it's not fair."

But Republicans blasted the proposal as an example of misguided economic policy that would ultimately harm consumers by discouraging investment in domestic energy production.

"This is Economics 101," said Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Kentucky. "You don't lower gas prices by punishing the companies that produce gas. This bill would do nothing to increase supply, nothing to lower prices, and everything to make America more dependent on foreign oil."

Sen. James Inhofe, R-Oklahoma, was more blunt in his assessment of the legislation.

"This isn't a serious energy policy — it's political theater," Inhofe said. "My colleagues on the other side of the aisle know this bill has no chance of actually lowering prices at the pump. They're playing politics with a crisis instead of offering real solutions like expanding domestic drilling."

Senate Republicans instead pushed for votes on expanding domestic oil exploration, including drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and offshore areas currently under moratorium — proposals that Democrats have long opposed on environmental grounds.

The White House also weighed in ahead of the vote, with press secretary Dana Perino saying President Bush would have vetoed the measure had it reached his desk.

"The president believes the way to bring down prices is to increase supply, not to demonize American energy companies," Perino said.

Oil industry representatives welcomed the bill's defeat. The American Petroleum Institute, the industry's largest trade group, issued a statement calling the proposal "counterproductive" and warning it would discourage the very investment needed to increase domestic energy production.

Despite Tuesday's setback, Democratic leaders vowed to continue pushing for action on energy prices, which have become an increasingly potent political issue ahead of the November elections.

"We are not giving up," Reid said. "The American people are hurting, and we will keep fighting for real relief at the pump."

Gasoline prices have risen sharply over the past year, with the national average hovering near $4 a gallon in many parts of the country — a level that has strained household budgets and emerged as a central issue in the presidential campaign.

Both presidential candidates, Sen. Barack Obama, D-Illinois, and Sen. John McCain, R-Arizona, have weighed in on energy policy in recent weeks, though they have offered starkly different approaches. Obama has expressed support for a windfall profits tax, while McCain has called for expanded offshore drilling and a temporary suspension of the federal gas tax.

With Congress set to leave for its summer recess in the coming weeks, it remains unclear whether lawmakers will revisit the issue before the November elections — though with gas prices continuing to dominate headlines and voter concerns, energy policy is likely to remain a flashpoint in Washington for months to come.

*CNN's congressional and political teams contributed to this report.*

# Senate Rejects Democratic Bid to Impose Windfall Tax on Oil Companies

**WASHINGTON** — A Democratic-led effort to impose a 25% windfall profits tax on major oil companies failed in the Senate this week, falling short of the votes needed to advance amid unified Republican opposition and defections from within the Democratic caucus.

The proposal, championed by progressive lawmakers, sought to levy the tax on oil companies reporting adjusted taxable income above $1 billion, with proceeds intended to be redistributed to consumers as rebates to offset high fuel costs. Sponsors argued the measure was necessary given record profits reported by major energy firms even as American households struggled with elevated gasoline and heating prices.

"These companies are posting historic profits while everyday Americans are choosing between filling their gas tank and putting food on the table," said one of the bill's lead sponsors during floor debate. "This is about basic fairness."

## Industry and GOP Pushback

Republicans and industry representatives argued the measure would backfire, potentially discouraging domestic production and investment at a time when energy security remains a pressing concern. Critics contended that a windfall tax could be passed along to consumers through higher prices rather than absorbed by corporations, undermining its stated purpose.

"This is not a serious solution — it's a political messaging bill," said the Senate Republican leader. "If you want lower prices at the pump, you increase supply. You don't punish the companies producing the energy Americans depend on."

Oil industry groups echoed these concerns, warning that punitive taxation could chill investment in future production and refining capacity, exacerbating long-term supply constraints.

## Vote Falls Short

The measure needed 60 votes to overcome a procedural hurdle but fell well short, with the tally largely following party lines. A handful of moderate Democrats joined Republicans in opposing the bill, citing concerns over its potential economic impact and questions about its constitutionality under provisions governing retroactive taxation.

The failed vote marks the second time in recent years that Democrats have attempted to advance windfall tax legislation targeting the oil sector, with similar efforts stalling amid concerns from moderates in the party.

## Reaction and Next Steps

Progressive advocacy groups expressed disappointment, vowing to continue pushing the issue ahead of upcoming elections. "Voters will remember who sided with Big Oil over their own constituents," said one advocacy group spokesperson.

Meanwhile, oil executives welcomed the outcome, with several companies noting that current profits are being reinvested into production, dividends, and shareholder returns.

The White House had signaled support for the measure but stopped short of aggressively lobbying for its passage, with administration officials instead emphasizing other strategies to address energy costs, including releases from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and diplomatic efforts to boost global supply.

With the bill's defeat, attention now turns to whether Democrats will attempt to attach similar provisions to broader legislative packages later in the session, though prospects for passage remain dim given the current partisan divide in the Senate.

*This report reflects a hypothetical legislative scenario for illustrative purposes.*

# Senate Rejects Bill to Strip Oil Companies of Tax Breaks

WASHINGTON — The Senate on Tuesday voted down legislation that would have eliminated approximately $2 billion in annual tax subsidies for the nation's largest oil companies, dealing a setback to Democrats who had hoped to capitalize on high gasoline prices and record industry profits to force a political showdown with Republicans.

The measure, which needed 60 votes to overcome procedural hurdles, fell largely along party lines, with most Republicans standing united against the proposal despite polls showing broad public support for repealing the tax breaks.

## Democrats Vow to Continue Fight

Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer expressed frustration with the outcome but signaled Democrats have no intention of abandoning the issue.

"The American people are struggling to fill their gas tanks while these companies are making more money than ever before in their history," Schumer said following the vote. "Republicans just told every family paying $4 or $5 a gallon at the pump that Big Oil's profits matter more than their pocketbooks. We are not going to let this go. We will bring this back again and again until Republicans join us in doing what's right for American families."

Schumer argued that closing the tax loopholes would help reduce the federal deficit while sending a message that Congress was responsive to consumer pain at the pump.

## Republicans Defend Vote as Sound Policy

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell dismissed the bill as political theater rather than serious energy policy, arguing it would do nothing to lower gas prices and could discourage domestic production.

"This is nothing more than a show vote designed to give our Democratic colleagues a talking point," McConnell said. "Punishing American energy producers with new taxes isn't going to bring the price of gas down by a single penny. If anything, it will discourage the very investment we need to increase domestic supply and reduce our reliance on foreign oil."

McConnell characterized the legislation as an attempt to distract from what he called the administration's broader energy policy failures, including restrictions on drilling permits and pipeline projects.

## Hutchison Cites Investment Concerns

Senator Kay Bailey Hutchison of Texas, a leading opponent of the bill, echoed concerns that removing the tax provisions would ultimately harm consumers by reducing incentives for companies to expand production.

"These are not subsidies unique to the oil and gas industry — many of these deductions are available to manufacturers across our economy," Hutchison said. "Singling out one industry for punitive tax treatment sends exactly the wrong signal at a time when we should be encouraging more American energy production, not less."

Hutchison, whose state is home to significant oil and gas operations, argued that the additional tax burden could translate into higher costs for consumers and reduced capital for exploration and drilling projects domestically.

## Political Stakes Ahead

The vote comes amid continued public frustration over gasoline prices and follows major oil companies reporting substantial quarterly profits, figures Democrats have repeatedly highlighted in press conferences and campaign messaging.

While the bill's failure was widely anticipated given the 60-vote threshold, Democratic strategists have suggested that forcing repeated votes on the issue could prove politically advantageous heading into future elections, putting Republican senators on record defending tax breaks for oil companies at a time of high energy costs.

Republicans, meanwhile, have sought to shift the conversation toward broader energy policy, calling for expanded drilling permits, pipeline approvals, and reduced regulatory barriers as more effective means of addressing prices at the pump.

With the two parties offering starkly different diagnoses — and prescriptions — for the nation's energy costs, the debate over oil industry taxation appears likely to resurface as both sides look to shape the narrative heading into the next election cycle.

# Windfall Profits Tax on Oil Companies Fails in Senate, Dealing Blow to Democrats' Energy Agenda

**WASHINGTON** — A closely watched bill that would have imposed a windfall profits tax on major oil companies failed to advance in the Senate Thursday, falling short of the 60 votes needed to overcome a Republican-led filibuster in a 51-47 vote that fell largely along party lines.

The legislation, which had been championed by progressive Democrats and the Biden administration amid soaring gasoline prices, would have imposed a 50% tax on the "excess" profits of companies producing or importing at least 300,000 barrels of oil per day. Revenue generated was intended to fund direct rebates to consumers struggling with pump prices.

## Bill's Key Provisions

The failed measure contained several notable components beyond the core tax mechanism:

**OPEC Legal Provisions**: The bill included language reviving elements of the long-stalled NOPEC (No Oil Producing and Exporting Cartels) Act, which would have opened the door for the Justice Department to pursue antitrust litigation against OPEC and its member nations for production quotas that critics argue artificially inflate global oil prices. Legal experts have long noted that such lawsuits would face significant hurdles, including sovereign immunity defenses, but supporters argued the mere threat of litigation could pressure OPEC+ nations to increase output.

**Strategic Petroleum Reserve Restrictions**: The legislation also sought to limit future SPR releases by requiring the Department of Energy to develop a formal replenishment strategy before any additional large-scale withdrawals could occur. This provision emerged after criticism—largely from Republicans—that the administration's historic SPR releases earlier this year had depleted the reserve to its lowest levels in decades without a clear plan for refilling it.

## Industry and Political Reaction

The American Petroleum Institute called the bill's defeat "a victory for common sense," with a spokesperson arguing that windfall taxes historically reduce domestic production incentives and could worsen supply constraints.

Senate Minority Leader statements characterized the bill as "political theater" designed to deflect blame from administration energy policies ahead of the midterms.

Proponents, including Senator Sheldon Whitehouse and progressive advocacy groups, expressed frustration but vowed to continue pushing the measure, possibly through reconciliation processes that would require only a simple majority.

## What Happens Next

With the bill's failure, attention now shifts to whether the administration will pursue additional unilateral executive actions on energy prices, including further SPR releases, export restriction discussions, or continued diplomatic pressure on OPEC+ producers ahead of their next scheduled output meeting.
